rationale: The specific quantitative claim that status epilepticus (HP:0002133) and focal/bilateral tonic-clonic seizures exceed 70% prevalence (>=25/35) while infantile epileptic spasms are present in <20% (<7/35) in the Leitão et al. dominant cohort is not supported by the available source text. Moreover, the proposed distinction between dominant DEE119 and recessive RNU2-2 encephalopathy based on status epilepticus fails because status epilepticus is also highly prevalent in biallelic recessive RNU2-2 DEE (57%, 8/14 patients in Henry et al. 2026), and Leitão et al. explicitly note that dominant and recessive RNU2-2 forms share overlapping clinical features.

evidence.text: Leitão et al. analyzed 141 individuals with RNU2-2 variants, including 35 with recurrent dominant pathogenic variants and 91 individuals with biallelic variants, noting that dominant and recessive RNU2-2 neurodevelopmental disorders share overlapping clinical features with frequent epilepsy, but the cohort data provided does not report that status epilepticus or focal/tonic-clonic seizures exceed 70% (>=25/35) or infantile spasms are <20% in the dominant subset.

source.title: Systematic analysis of snRNA genes reveals frequent RNU2-2 variants in dominant and recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
source.quote: We report RNU2-2 variants in 141 individuals, including 35 with recurrent dominant pathogenic variants and 91 affected members from 73 families with biallelic variants... Dominant and recessive RNU2-2 NDDs share overlapping clinical features, with frequent epilepsy.

evidence.text: In dominant RNU2-2 DEE reported by Chiu et al., all 5 patients had status epilepticus (both convulsive and nonconvulsive) with median seizure onset of 24 months, focal and generalized seizures, hyperventilation, and obstructive sleep apnea.

source.title: Pathogenic Variants in RNU2‐2, a Non‐coding Spliceosomal RNA, Cause a Distinctive Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy
source.quote: Patients with RNU2-2 DEE had median seizure onset age of 24 months, focal and generalized seizures, status epilepticus (n = 5), severe to profound impairment, hyperventilation (n = 3), and obstructive sleep apnea (n = 3).

evidence.text: Greene et al. identified recurrent de novo mutations at positions 4 and 35 of RNU2-2 across 25 individuals with severe neurodevelopmental disorder, reporting seizures in 89% along with microcephaly, hypotonia, and hyperventilation, without specific subcohort frequency demonstrating status epilepticus in >=25/35.

source.title: Mutations in the small nuclear RNA gene RNU2-2 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent epilepsy
source.quote: ‘Seizure’ was annotated in 89% of RNU2-2... recurrent de novo single-nucleotide mutations at nucleotide positions 4 and 35 of RNU2-2 in nine cases. We replicated this finding in 16 additional cases, bringing the total to 25.

conflicts: The hypothesis posits that status epilepticus distinguishes dominant DEE119 from recessive RNU2-2 encephalopathy, but Henry et al. (2026) report that status epilepticus occurred in 57% (8/14) of recessive cases.
The specific numerators and thresholds (>=25/35 status epilepticus, <7/35 infantile spasms) are unverified and absent from the available text of Leitão et al.

new_directions.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for specific seizure semiologies (infantile spasms vs. focal/bilateral tonic-clonic seizures vs. status epilepticus) across the full 35 dominant RNU2-2 patients in Leitão et al.?
new_directions.rationale: A comprehensive table extracted from the full clinical supplement of Leitão et al. is required to establish whether seizure semiology statistically differs between dominant and recessive RNU2-2 cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: Does median age of seizure onset (e.g. 24 months in dominant vs. early infancy in recessive) provide better phenotypic discrimination than status epilepticus occurrence?
new_directions.rationale: Chiu et al. reported an onset age around 24 months in dominant cases, whereas recessive cohorts manifest with early-infancy spasms, suggesting onset timing rather than status epilepticus alone may be the discriminating feature.
